title: 📘 UNIT 3: NATURAL RESOURCES AND CONFLICTS OVER RESOURCES
notes: Natural resources are materials and environmental assets that support human life, livelihoods and economic activities.

title: 🌍 3.1 THE FUNCTIONS AND MANAGEMENT OF LAND
notes:
Land is a broad concept that can be viewed as a resource, environment, legal object, economic asset and cultural wealth.

🌱 Land provides :-
🔹 Food
🔹 Shelter
🔹 Space for production and settlement
🔹 Ecosystem functions
🔹 Economic and cultural benefits

⭐ Land is the foundation of human activities and supports both biotic and abiotic components of the environment.

title: 🌱 3.1.1 LAND RESOURCES
notes:
Land resources are usable materials naturally occurring in the environment. They are derived from the lithosphere, biosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere.

📌 Classification by regeneration :-
♻️ Renewable resources :- can regenerate or be replenished after use.
⛏️ Non-renewable resources :- finite resources that do not regenerate quickly.

📌 Other classifications :-
🔹 Biotic and abiotic
🔹 Stock and flow
🔹 Ubiquitous, unique, common and rare
🔹 Potential, actual and conditional resources.

title: ♻️ 3.1.2 RENEWABLE AND NON-RENEWABLE RESOURCES
notes:
♻️ Renewable resources :- can replace themselves when the rate of use is lower than the rate of regeneration and the environment is protected.

Examples :- plants, animals, crops and forests.

⚠️ Renewable does not mean impossible to exhaust. Excessive use can deplete renewable resources.

⛏️ Non-renewable resources :- exist in limited quantities and regenerate extremely slowly.

Examples :- minerals, coal and petroleum.

⭐ Management :- sustainable use, recycling and reuse where possible.

title: 🌿 3.1.3 LAND AS AN ENVIRONMENT
notes:
Land as an environment includes the biotic and abiotic components found on, above and below Earth's surface.

It includes :-
🌱 Plants and animals
🌬️ Atmospheric gases
🪨 Geology and rocks
🌾 Soils
💧 Hydrology
👥 Human activities

⭐ Ecological role :- land supports breeding and survival of organisms and can also serve as a sink for wastes.

title: ⚙️ 3.1.4 FUNCTIONS OF LAND
notes:
Land performs several important functions :-

🏭 Production function :- serves as a means of production.

♻️ Waste-disposal function :- acts as a sink for wastes.

💰 Economic function :- can be converted into capital and economic assets.

🏛️ Cultural function :- provides places for traditional, cultural and religious activities.

⭐ Land therefore has environmental, economic, social and cultural importance.

title: 🛡️ 3.1.5 LAND MANAGEMENT
notes:
Land management :- proper use and protection of land resources to provide benefits to present and future populations while maintaining ecosystem services.

🎯 Main objective :- control land degradation and balance resource exploitation with regeneration.

Important practices :-
🌳 Afforestation and reforestation
🌾 Proper farming practices
🐄 Controlled grazing
🏔️ Terracing
💧 Check-damming
🌱 Soil and water conservation
⚡ Use of renewable energy

⭐ Effective management should consider local needs, indigenous knowledge, culture, economy and politics.

title: ⚠️ 3.2 RESOURCES UNDER PRESSURE
notes:
Rapid population growth and increased human demand place strong pressure on natural resources.

The most heavily pressured renewable land resources include :-
🌱 Soil
💧 Freshwater
🌳 Forests

These are often common-pool resources and can suffer from the 'tragedy of the commons' when individuals overuse shared resources.

⛏️ Non-renewable resources under pressure include :-
🔹 Fossil fuels
🔹 Minerals
🔹 Gold
🔹 Diamonds

⭐ Major pressure :- population growth, urbanization, migration, agriculture, energy demand and resource exploitation.

title: 🌱 3.2.1 SOIL RESOURCES
notes:
Soil is an essential agricultural and environmental resource, but excessive use and erosion reduce its quality.

Major causes of soil depletion :-
🔹 Loss of nutrients
🔹 Removal of topsoil
🔹 Reduction of soil organisms
🔹 Crusting and compaction
🔹 Pollution
🔹 Salinity

Three major forms :-
🪨 Physical :- crusting, compaction and reduced soil depth.
🧪 Chemical :- salinization, alkalinization and acidification.
🦠 Biological :- loss of soil organisms and decline of soil organic carbon.

⭐ Effect :- reduced agricultural productivity and loss of ecosystem functions.

title: 💧 3.2.2 WATER RESOURCES
notes:
Water is essential for humans, animals, plants and ecosystems.

It contributes to :-
🌱 Plant growth
🪨 Soil formation and rock weathering
♻️ Organic matter decomposition
🌧️ Rainfall processes
⚡ Power generation
🌊 Aquatic ecosystems

⚠️ Major threats :-
🔹 Domestic and industrial waste
🔹 Plastic pollution
🔹 Water hyacinth
🔹 Oil spills
🔹 Industrial chemicals
🔹 Increasing water demand
🔹 Drought and climate change

⭐ Water scarcity is especially serious in many arid and semi-arid regions.

title: 🌳 3.2.3 FOREST RESOURCES
notes:
Forests are major terrestrial ecosystems that provide many ecosystem services and support wildlife and human livelihoods.

Major pressures :-
🔹 Population growth
🔹 Agricultural expansion
🔹 Livestock production
🔹 Demand for fuelwood and timber
🔹 Plantation agriculture
🔹 Mining
🔹 Urbanization
🔹 Biofuel demand
🔹 Climate change
🔹 Changing consumption patterns

⭐ Forest loss threatens biodiversity, livelihoods, soil protection and environmental stability.

title: 🌳 3.2.4 FOREST CONSERVATION
notes:
Important forest-management measures :-

🌱 Afforestation :- planting trees on land that was not previously forested.

🌳 Reforestation :- replanting trees in deforested areas.

🛡️ Soil and Water Conservation :- integrating forest protection with SWC activities.

⚡ Alternative energy :- hydropower, solar and wind can reduce pressure for fuelwood.

👥 Participatory forest management :- involving local users in decision-making.

📚 Education and awareness :- improving understanding of sustainable forest use.

💧 Watershed management :- protecting watersheds and their resources.

🇪🇹 Ethiopia example :- Green Legacy.

title: ⛏️ 3.2.5 NON-RENEWABLE RESOURCES UNDER PRESSURE
notes:
Non-renewable resources under intense pressure include :-

🛢️ Fossil fuels :- oil and coal.
💎 Precious minerals :- gold and diamonds.

🔹 Their formation is extremely slow.
🔹 Excessive extraction reduces their availability.
🔹 Competition over valuable resources can contribute to conflicts among groups and countries.

🌍 Examples of regions affected by resource-related conflicts include parts of the Middle East, Central Africa and West Africa.

title: 🏜️ 3.3 LAND RESOURCE DEPLETION AND DEGRADATION
notes:
Resource degradation :- overall decline in the quality and quantity of land resources such as soil, water and biological resources.

It may result from :-
👥 Human activities
🌋 Natural hazards

Natural hazards mentioned include earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides and floods.

⭐ Degradation reduces resource productivity and environmental quality.

title: 📉 3.3.1 CAUSES OF RESOURCE DEGRADATION
notes:
Causes can be divided into underlying and proximate causes.

🔹 Underlying causes :- major forces that create conditions for degradation.

Examples :-
👥 Rapid population growth
🍚 Increased demand for food
🌾 Increased demand for farmland
🔥 Increased demand for biomass energy and timber
🐄 Increased demand for pasture
🌡️ Climate change

🔹 Proximate causes :- direct activities that produce degradation.

Examples :-
🌾 Intensive land use
🌳 Deforestation
🐄 Overstocking and overgrazing
🌱 Removal of vegetation
🏜️ Desertification.

title: 💥 3.3.2 CONSEQUENCES OF RESOURCE DEGRADATION
notes:
Major consequences include :-

🌱 Loss of soil fertility
🌾 Reduced agricultural productivity
🌳 Forest-cover reduction
💧 Water pollution
🌬️ Air pollution
🏜️ Desertification
🌿 Loss of vegetation cover
💰 Increased poverty
🌡️ Greater environmental vulnerability

⭐ Resource degradation can create a cycle where declining resources reduce livelihoods and increasing poverty places further pressure on resources.

title: 🛠️ 3.3.3 RESOURCE CONSERVATION MEASURES
notes:
Important land and resource-management practices include :-

🌳 Afforestation :- planting trees on barren land.
🌲 Reforestation :- replanting deforested areas.
🚫 Area closure :- protecting degraded areas from livestock to allow recovery.
🏔️ Terracing :- reducing runoff and trapping soil.
🧱 Check-dams :- reducing water velocity and controlling erosion.
🌾 Mulching :- covering soil with plant residues to conserve moisture and improve nutrients.
🌬️ Shelterbelts :- reducing wind speed and wind erosion.
💧 Diversion canals :- diverting floodwater.
🕳️ Trenches :- trapping water and soil.
🚰 Drainage channels :- removing excess water.
🌱 Legume rotation :- restoring soil fertility.
🐄 Animal manure :- replacing lost nutrients.
🌾 Intercropping :- improving soil fertility and land use.
💧 Proper irrigation :- reducing salinity problems.
🧪 Fertilizers and green manure :- maintaining soil fertility.

title: 🌊 3.4 TRANSBOUNDARY RIVERS
notes:
Transboundary rivers :- watercourses shared by two or more countries.

Transboundary waters include :-
🌊 Rivers
🏞️ Lakes
💧 Inland waters
🕳️ Aquifers

🌍 The textbook identifies more than 263 transnational river and lake channels plus numerous trans-state aquifers.

⭐ These shared waters cross national boundaries and require cooperation among riparian countries.

title: 🌍 3.4.1 DISTRIBUTION OF TRANSBOUNDARY WATERCOURSES
notes:
Transboundary watercourses are widely distributed around the world.

📌 They make up about 60% of global freshwater flows and cover nearly half of Earth's terrestrial surface.

📌 They cross the territories of about 145 nations and support roughly 40% of the global population.

📌 About 60% of Africa and South America and nearly 40% of North and Central America fall within international river systems.

⭐ Shared water resources therefore have major global economic, social and environmental importance.

title: 🤝 3.4.2 PROSPECTS OF TRANSBOUNDARY WATERCOURSES
notes:
Shared rivers can promote cooperation and development.

Benefits include :-
💧 Water supply
🌾 Agriculture
⚡ Hydropower
🚢 Navigation
🏭 Industry
🧼 Sanitation
🐟 Ecosystem services
💰 Economic development
🤝 Regional cooperation
🕊️ Peace and security

⭐ Shared watercourses can connect countries economically, socially and environmentally.

title: ⚠️ 3.4.3 CHALLENGES OF SHARED RIVERS
notes:
Shared rivers may also create tensions when countries have different interests.

Possible problems :-
🔹 Competition over water use
🔹 Irrigation demands
🔹 Hydropower development
🔹 Water shortages
🔹 Pollution
🔹 Rapid population growth
🔹 Poor management
🔹 Lack of cooperation

⭐ Therefore, transboundary rivers can become both sources of cooperation and sources of conflict.

title: 🗺️ 3.4.4 MAJOR SHARED RIVER BASINS
notes:
Important examples of international river basins include :-

🌊 Nile :- shared by 11 riparian countries.
🌊 Congo :- shared by 11 countries.
🌊 Zambezi :- shared by 8 countries.
🌊 Niger :- shared by several West African countries.
🌊 Danube :- passes through the territories of 19 countries.
🌊 Ganges :- shared by 4 countries.
🌊 Mekong :- shared by 6 countries.
🌊 Rhine :- shared by 9 countries.
🌊 Okavango :- shared by 4 countries.

⭐ The number of riparian states makes cooperation essential for sustainable river management.

title: 🇪🇹 3.4.5 THE NILE BASIN AND ETHIOPIA
notes:
The Nile River is shared by 11 riparian countries and supports millions of people.

🇪🇹 Ethiopia contributes more than 85% of the Nile's water according to the textbook.

Major uses of Nile water include :-
🌾 Irrigation
⚡ Hydropower
💧 Water supply

🇪🇹🇸🇩🇪🇬 Ethiopia, Sudan and Egypt have important interests in the use and development of Nile waters.

⭐ The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) is presented as an important example of the opportunities and contentions surrounding Nile water development.

title: 🤝 3.5 REGIONAL COOPERATION FOR SUSTAINABLE USE OF SHARED RIVERS
notes:
Shared river basins require agreements and institutions because different countries may have different priorities and interests.

🎯 Main purpose of regional cooperation :-
🔹 Coordinate water use.
🔹 Promote sustainable development.
🔹 Reduce disputes.
🔹 Protect ecosystems.
🔹 Improve regional peace and security.

⭐ Effective management requires cooperation among riparian states and appropriate regional institutions.

title: 🏛️ 3.5.1 REGIONAL INSTITUTIONS
notes:
Regional institutions help countries coordinate the use and management of shared natural resources.

They can :-
🔹 Establish common rules.
🔹 Facilitate negotiation.
🔹 Encourage information sharing.
🔹 Coordinate development activities.
🔹 Support environmental protection.
🔹 Reduce potential conflicts.

⭐ Shared resources are more effectively managed through formal cooperation than through unilateral actions.

title: 🌊 3.5.2 NILE COOPERATION AND INSTITUTIONS
notes:
The textbook discusses several important Nile-related agreements and institutions.

📌 Nile Basin Initiative (NBI) :- promotes cooperation among Nile Basin countries.

📌 Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) :- seeks cooperation on sustainable development and management of the Nile Basin.

📌 Joint institutions and technical arrangements :- support consultation and management among participating states.

⭐ Cooperation aims to achieve mutual benefit, sustainable development and peaceful management of shared waters.

title: ⚔️ 3.6 CONFLICTS OVER RESOURCES
notes:
Natural resource conflict :- conflict arising from competition over the control, ownership or use of natural resources.

Common resources involved :-
🌍 Land
🌳 Timber
💧 Freshwater
⛏️ Minerals
⚡ Energy
🛢️ Hydrocarbons
🐟 Fishing resources

⭐ When resources become scarce, valuable or unevenly controlled, competition among users can intensify.

title: 🔥 3.6.1 CAUSES OF RESOURCE CONFLICT
notes:
Major causes include :-

🔹 Resource scarcity
🔹 Competition over ownership and control
🔹 Rapid population growth
🔹 Poor resource management
🔹 Policy failures
🔹 Lack of transparency
🔹 Inequitable resource distribution
🔹 Political interests
🔹 Environmental degradation
🔹 Competition between communities or countries

⭐ Scarcity combined with unequal access and weak institutions increases the likelihood of conflict.

title: 💥 3.6.2 CONSEQUENCES OF RESOURCE CONFLICT
notes:
Resource conflicts can result in :-

⚠️ Political instability
🌳 Further resource degradation
🏚️ Loss of livelihoods
💰 Economic losses
👥 Social disruption
🗺️ Regional fragmentation
🤝 Breakdown of cooperation

⭐ Conflict can further damage the resources that communities depend on, creating a cycle of scarcity and competition.

title: 🕊️ 3.6.3 CONFLICT MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES
notes:
Common approaches to managing conflicts include :-

🚫 Avoidance :- preventing a conflict from becoming openly confrontational.

💪 Coercion :- using or threatening force to impose one's will.

🤝 Negotiation :- parties voluntarily reach an agreement through discussion.

⚖️ Arbitration :- a mutually accepted third party makes a decision.

🕊️ Mediation :- a third party facilitates negotiations without imposing a solution.

🏛️ Adjudication :- a judge or authorized administrator makes a binding decision.

⭐ Peaceful dialogue and negotiation are especially important for shared natural resources.

title: 💧 3.6.4 PRINCIPLES FOR SHARED RIVER CONFLICTS
notes:
Conflicts over shared rivers can be reduced through :-

🤝 Equitable use of the basin.
🛡️ Avoiding significant harm to other riparian states.
⚖️ Respecting sovereign equality and territorial integrity.
📢 Sharing relevant information.
🗣️ Consulting other riparian states.
🔔 Giving prior notification before major actions.
🌱 Joint environmental protection.
🕊️ Resolving disputes through dialogue and negotiation.

⭐ Cooperation, transparency and fairness are key to sustainable shared-water management.

title: 🧠 UNIT 3 KEY CONCEPTS
notes:
🌍 Land :- foundation of human activity and an important natural resource.

♻️ Renewable resource :- can regenerate when properly managed.

⛏️ Non-renewable resource :- finite and regenerates extremely slowly.

📉 Resource degradation :- decline in the quality and quantity of resources.

🌱 Soil degradation :- physical, chemical or biological decline of soil quality.

💧 Water stress :- pressure caused by increasing demand and limited water supply.

🌳 Afforestation :- planting trees on land without previous forest cover.

🌲 Reforestation :- replanting trees in deforested areas.

🌊 Transboundary river :- river shared by two or more countries.

🤝 Riparian states :- countries sharing a river or watercourse.

⚔️ Resource conflict :- competition or dispute over natural-resource control, ownership or use.

🕊️ Mediation :- third party facilitates negotiation without imposing a decision.

⚖️ Arbitration :- third party provides a decision accepted by the parties.

🏛️ Adjudication :- binding decision by a judge or administrator.

title: ⭐ UNIT 3 QUICK REVISION
notes:
📌 Land is a resource, environment, economic asset and cultural asset.

📌 Natural resources can be classified in several ways, including renewable/non-renewable and biotic/abiotic.

📌 Renewable resources can still be depleted through excessive use.

📌 Land management aims to balance resource exploitation with regeneration.

📌 Soil, water and forests are among the renewable resources under greatest human pressure.

📌 Soil degradation may be physical, chemical or biological.

📌 Major resource-degradation causes include population growth, intensive land use, deforestation, overgrazing and climate change.

📌 Conservation methods include afforestation, reforestation, terracing, check-dams, mulching, shelterbelts, crop rotation, manure and proper irrigation.

📌 Transboundary waters are shared by two or more countries.

📌 Shared rivers provide opportunities for agriculture, hydropower, navigation, water supply and regional cooperation.

📌 They can also create disputes because countries may have competing interests.

📌 The Nile is shared by 11 riparian countries and is an important example of both cooperation and contention.

📌 Regional institutions and agreements help manage shared rivers sustainably.

📌 Resource conflicts may result from scarcity, unequal access, poor management, policy failures and lack of transparency.

📌 Conflict-management methods include avoidance, coercion, negotiation, arbitration, mediation and adjudication.

⭐ Core idea :- Natural resources support human life and development, but increasing pressure, degradation and unequal access can create conflict. Sustainable management and cooperation are essential.
